cutting-mother.songLyrics:

Don't fear—papa's here, I'm pullin' up from the rear.

Duck, clown—look round.

I'm clean now.

Break (Silence / Breath)
{Long breath}

I'm ready to seek, I'm ready to peak.
I'm ready to freak any day of the week—
Forward motion, no retreat.

{Long breath}

Outro (Spoken)
Cut complete.
Signal live.

cutting-mother.interpretation:
Severance as initiation. The poem stages separation from inherited identity ("cutting mother") as both violent and necessary. Creativity arrives through rupture: danger, breathlessness, manic discovery, self-reinvention.

The speaker oscillates between confidence ("I'm clean now") and destabilization (brain busts, urge to run/hide/seek). Violence is metaphorical—language for psychic cutting, not harm.

Emotional vector: rupture → exhilaration → disorientation → readiness.

blame-dad.interpretation:
Intergenerational wound processing. Desire is framed as absence—wanting what was never received. Anger, shame, and unmet needs loop somatically before cognition catches up. "Blame Dad" is less accusation than shorthand for origin pain.

The poem pivots from reactive blame to regulation: noticing heat, sweat, impulses; interrupting patterns at the seed. Vulnerability replaces strength; honesty replaces dominance.

The ending destabilizes aggression mid-sentence, revealing awareness in real time.

Emotional vector: resentment → somatic surge → humility → self-interruption.

pride-suicide.interpretation:
Ego collapse staged as bravado. The speaker performs excess—sexual, social, linguistic—while admitting loneliness, repetition, and depletion. Pride is both armor and noose; clout substitutes for connection, then fails under scarcity.

Humor and wordplay mask vulnerability until the admission lands: the system built to survive drought cannot tolerate it.

Emotional vector: swagger → confession → exposure → clarity through failure.

isuck.title: iSuck
isuck.lyrics: Yo, I suck. I mean I can't do this. This whole thing. This whole rap game. This whole Instafame, Insta-fucking strain…on the brain. Let's get depressed. Self-pity, self-absorption, self-importance. Let's take a selfie. It's healthy, could make you wealthy, makes sense. But be stealthy...not dense. You cover that shit up, and swing for the fence. I mean you're doing it for the music. You're doing for it for the art. Don't start. Can't stop. Groove this. There's no doubt we got some money on the table. So unstable and unable, swallow fable, and enabled the mislabel. Spin the dreidel, you lucky son of a gun. You won! 14 likes, 3 comments, a new follower. Home run!
isuck.interpretation:
Self-sabotage as performance critique. The speaker oscillates between raw self-rejection and cynical awareness of attention economics. "Sucking" is less incompetence than exhaustion under visibility pressure: Instafame compresses identity into metrics.

Authenticity is claimed, then immediately undercut by incentives—likes, comments, followers. Art-versus-algorithm tension drives the piece.

Humor masks anxiety; bravado collapses into scorekeeping.

Emotional vector: confession → irony → manic validation. The ending exposes the trap: winning feels empty but still counts.

quid-pro-quo.interpretation:

Momentum versus suffocation: stored power becomes blockage. Speech creates irreversible consequence; debt accrues internally, not financially.

Braggadocio is present but unstable—proof, growth, flight—cut by domestic imagery and bodily needs.

The final turn rejects empty talk and misaligned collaboration.

Emotional tone: sharp skepticism, pressured pride, fatigue, self-awareness.

Drive: confront the exchange rate of loyalty, words, and energy.

The text oscillates between self-critique and ego armor—bravado as a coping mechanism, humor as deflection.

Core tension: wanting to speak from origin while addicted to performance. The ending punctures the persona—confidence acknowledged, then dismissed as irrelevant.

Emotional tone: restless, self-aware, slightly manic, honest underneath noise.

blue collar on the rise so send your kids to college without wearing ties but still thirsting for knowledge
America was confident and life was good
As long as you did, basically, exactly what you fucking should
Black people are free, but better stay in their place
That shit was the norm, not really questioning race
Black support came from your home and family
Best not civil rights yourself too damn unhappily
Massive resistance and a hero in Martin Luther King bring
A reason to think and see and really sing for something
Shout out to Eisenhower, you know my boy, Dwight D.
Shout out to Harry Truman…well, of course, you agree
New suburbs, everybody forget the forgotten war
The Korean war, McCarthy says cold is war
Communists aren't people
Just some great evil

Atomic bombs, duck and cover, bomb shelter
Don't question our America mmmk, be Uncle Sam's big helper
So was America great then? Did that greatness give way?
Was it better being a white guy? Who am I to say?
During World War II women had entered the work force in record numbers, but now that the war was over, many returned home and their jobs became being mothers.

1950s-america.interpretation:
A panoramic audit of the 1950s mythos. Nostalgia is invoked, then stress-tested. The poem catalogs innocence, consumer novelty, teen energy, and postwar confidence—then overlays exclusion, repression, propaganda, disease, and fear.

It refuses simple moral accounting. Progress and cruelty coexist. The voice is observational, not sentimental: admiration without blindness, critique without anachronistic scolding.

The closing image—water flowing downstream—frames history as inheritance rather than verdict.

Emotional tone: animated curiosity → ironic distance → sober integration.

Kissing and lovemaking?

dating.interpretation:
Exploratory vulnerability. Dating is framed as a liminal practice: awkward, hopeful, performative, honest by turns. The speaker toggles between casual process and archetypal longing—skill-building versus soul-mate fantasy.

Humor softens fear of rejection; lists mirror trial-and-error learning. The final question suspends certainty and control, inviting consent without demand.

Emotional vector: curiosity → self-awareness → aspiration → open-ended permission.

poly-jesus.songLyrics:

Oh fuck.

Damn this beat just suck—nip and tuck, uppercut, chin to gut.
Nut butter, butternut, squash you, Tosh you, posh crew, mosh you,
Accost you—yeah, I sauced you.

Verse 2 (Spoken, escalating)
Possibly the best MC this side NC,
Jake G, bragadociously, precociously.
Toast with glee, quite possibly I knock MCs,

Balkin' while I'm talkin', in walks Christopher Walken—

Eyes bugged out, hands double Spockin'.

What the fawk I'm doin', screwin',

Chewin' glue, poo-in', new stew, queue-in'

New fright, brew bite, a few might—

{Silence}

All these words meant to do is fill some bars,

You could be rude.
Could say please.
Lookin' for the thing that pleases.

poly-jesus.interpretation:
Manic overflow resolving into a single lucid question. The poem intentionally floods language—braggadocio, nonsense syllables, pop intrusion, verbal percussion—to exhaust ego performance. The excess is the point: bars as filler, motion without meaning, until a quiet insight cuts through.

"Poly Jesus" is not theology; it's a hunger for distributed forgiveness, non-exclusive grace, relief from binary judgment. The speaker moves from dominance and chaos to humility and asking.

Emotional vector: frenzy → self-awareness → moral longing.

rip-current.title: Rip Current
rip-current.songLyrics:
Intro (Spoken)
Rip current.

Verse 1 (Flowing spoken)
Philosophically velocity impossibly on top of me,
I drop a beat, I hop the street, I stop and pee,

Ever face me, erasing after chasing, not tasty.

Había una chica, un día me gustaría llamar la policía,

Icy cold stare, frigid air hit the underwear,
Wear under my blunder, thundered, put asunder.
Boy wonder wondered, stun gun stunned her,
Turned and mumbled, "bummer."

Verse 3 (Spoken, slightly darker)
Lonely summer, dumber than the one-armed drummer,
Gave her everything I had
'Cause I wanted something from her.
Fun hurt, sunburnt, you learnt, they turned—
Out to be the first degree of a rip current.

Break (Silence)

Outro (Spoken, clear and steady)
A relatively strong, narrow current
Flowing outward from the beach,
Through the surf zone,
Presenting a hazard to swimmers.
rip-current.interpretation:
Momentum without control. The poem moves like water that looks playful until it isn't. Language accelerates, slips, multilingual fragments appear, social misreads stack, desire overreaches, generosity masks extraction, and suddenly the force turns outward.

"Rip current" becomes the governing metaphor: attraction plus ego plus confusion pulling someone away from safety while feeling like movement. The final definition reframes the whole piece—what felt like agency was a hazard.

Emotional vector: kinetic play → social misfire → self-exposure → conceptual clarity.

hangin-with-myself.interpretation:
Self-attachment as stability. The poem reframes solitude as chosen companionship rather than lack. Routine anchors the week; self-care, creativity, parenting, desire, and humor coexist without apology. The exaggerated flirtation with oneself is playful, not narcissistic—an assertion that availability to one's own energy precedes healthy intimacy with others.

Emotional vector: grounded routine → self-amusement → warmth → affirmation.

forces-inside-me.interpretation:
Multiplicity without a controller. Treats identity as a dynamic field where forces arise and dissolve—hope and doubt coexisting, agency appearing moment-to-moment rather than as a fixed "I." Resolution is not certainty but bowing to the moment, refusing to fossilize perspective.

Emotional vector: playful entrance → existential curiosity → cyclical becoming → grounded humility.

The "attack" language is theatrical pressure, a way to break through sleep, avoidance, and self-mythologized brokenness. What looks like aggression is actually insistence: you are needed, and hiding is no longer convincing.

The core tension is silence versus speech. The addressee is "up to your neck with the unspoken," actively sustaining suffering by rehearsing a story of being damaged. Self-pity isn't portrayed as weakness but as a kind of addiction—warm, steamy, familiar—contrasted with the risk of movement and exposure.

Mentorship appears as foreknowledge: others saw this person's capacity early, before fatigue and creases set in. The "town waiting" signals community, responsibility, and participation—life happening without you if you stay asleep.

The hitchhiker image reframes the moral: nothing carries you forward for free. Payment isn't transactional in a literal sense; it's existential. You either offer honesty, effort, or vulnerability—or you stay stranded.

At bottom, the poem is not about power over someone. It's about calling someone back into motion.

The question it leaves hanging is simple and uncomfortable: Will you speak, or will you keep paying the cost of silence?

biography.title: Biography
biography.interpretation:
A four-movement arc of a life. Movement I traces becoming—birth, childhood play, cultural inheritance, and the first stirrings of constraint within dreams. Movement II charts overreach and fracture—borrowed confidence, travel, consequence, loss of brothers, and the stubborn sense that something remains unfound. Movement III turns toward stewardship—grown sons, new babies, business, the body breaking, art emerging from sustained pressure. Movement IV arrives at return—inward territory, no separation left to mend, gratitude, and service as the quieter yes.

The refrain evolves across movements: from observation ("Everything begins / Everything will end") to acceptance ("Everything must end") to settled presence ("Everything begins / Everything ends"). The outro lands simply: "And still… we live."

Emotional arc: emergence → experimentation → rupture → responsibility → release → return.

midwife-my-life.title: Midwife My Life
midwife-my-life.interpretation:
The piece frames growth not as rescue or self-mastery but as a human process of emergence—being witnessed, supported, and allowed rather than fixed or forced. It moves from vulnerability and surrender into the recognition that struggle is not failure but evidence of life in motion, and that guidance is relational, grounded, and humane. The closing line—"at least that's what they promised at the self-help convention"—then deliberately undercuts the sacred tone, introducing irony that exposes how even authentic insights are often commodified and sold as guarantees. This final turn prevents the work from becoming doctrine or self-help scripture, returns authority to lived experience, and leaves the listener suspended between sincerity and skepticism, truth and marketing—keeping the meaning embodied, unresolved, and human.

Emotional arc: vulnerability → surrender → emergence → ironic undercutting → suspended meaning.
